sections.title: Introduction (Overview)
sections.content:
# Introduction (Overview)

<!-- chapter: 01-introduction | pages: 3-3 -->

CH I. Introduction to Reverie
Have you ever stepped into the planar edge? It feels like standing on the border
between dream and wake. It is a place where impossible landscapes begin to form
before your eyes while your deeply held fears manifest behind your back. There is
nothing out there but your thoughts waiting to be given form. We’ve lived in our little
bubble for centuries, enough to almost forget there was once more to the world than
this tiny pocket of misery would have you believe. One thing is for certain though –
once the Purities set their minds to finally exploring what lies beyond, they will either
force their way through the veil or kill us all in the attempt.

sections.title: The System
sections.content:
# The System

<!-- chapter: 01-introduction | pages: 3-5 -->

Reverie is a game about tortured people dealing with their internal struggles in a
world that manifests them into reality. These “souls” navigate unstable pockets of
space where sentient minds dictate reality, they sacrifice and fight for those they
represent and they meet horrible fates when they get stuck between pragmatism
and integrity. The setting of Dunyor is a mix of gothic and new weird fantasy with
various philosophical and metaphysical themes layered throughout. Reverie will be
at its best in long lasting campaigns centered around the moral and ethical
alignment of its main cast as they bend or break in tragic fashion.
Reverie is a game about many things, but the most important are the following:
● Conviction - Reverie was designed to make roleplaying a character with
defined beliefs as fun and engaging as possible. Your characters’ personal
beliefs will influence everything from skill checks to combat, from mundane
interactions to the fabric of reality.
● Sacrifice - Where other narratives may focus on noble, capable heroes,
Reverie instead showcases what heroism costs. Heroes do exist, but they
rarely if ever end up being rewarded for their pursuits. Their powers always
come at a horrible cost, and by choosing to be heroic they are going against
their own well-being and happiness in a desperate attempt to provide them
for others. More often than not, characters in Reverie are just competent
people put into situations way above their capabilities.
● Sorrow - While you will feel many things throughout the game, the emotion
that will consistently be the most central is sorrow. Sadness has a way of
lowering our guard and making us more open to deep thought and
reconsideration of our beliefs. We will explore it and we will consider its
painful realities. These stories will be hopeful tragedies.

It should also be noted what Reverie is explicitly not:
● A crunchfest - despite having many rules for many things, Reverie’s rules are
there to serve the narrative rather than the other way around. They are to be
ignored if they would conflict with the story or hinder the tone, though they
are designed with the intent to avoid this as much as possible. The various
systems and procedures are there to create friction and tension in order to
set the mood at the table. The most impactful moments of gameplay will be
narrative situations enabled and foretold by mechanical realities.
● A social relaxation game - More often than not, Reverie expects you to be
fully invested into the world and the story. Roleplay is heavily encouraged
because it naturally fits the melancholic tone. The game’s central themes are
heavy and demand to be taken seriously by the players. If you are sensitive to
stories about hardship and death or if you are looking for a simple way to
pass time with a group of friends, I recommend you take a look at any of the
great games designed to provide just that.
● An escapist fantasy - While beautiful and hopeful moments exist and are
essential to the experience, they are not the norm. If you want to play a game
to escape from your real life, you should be aware that many topics in Reverie
will pull you into just that. Politics and ideology play a big part in most
narratives and the game intends to ask you, the player, how far your own
beliefs could stretch and how horrible they could become before you stop to
reconsider. This may not suit everyone, and for those I suggest a more
light-hearted game.
***
With all that in mind, if you are not repulsed by these commitments, if you believe
that you can handle some introspection and if you desire to be a part of a game and
story that takes itself and its audience seriously, enter and be welcomed.

The World
The various planes of Dunyor are split apart by unreality, a void where the laws of
space and time stop functioning. The planes themselves are stable pockets of
existence shaped by their distance from the world’s Origin point and by the Seasons
its inhabitants adhere to.
The world’s Seasons define its conditions, each represented by 4 differing
convictions, each manifesting in a different way. Those devoted to them, Virtues,
have the ability to channel them directly and bend the fragile reality. Individuals
embodying each of them the most are known as Purities and they are the closest
thing to gods this world has seen. Their bodies are warped and their minds
inflexible, they act as the living executors of the will of the metaphysical Seasons.
421 years after the event that shattered Dunyor, the inhabitants of Eterion,
confident that they have enough knowledge on how to traverse the void, send out
the First March, an expedition into this strange new world, the first of many, in
order to survey its people, to secure new resources in order to avoid the collapse of
their plane and to find out what happened all those centuries ago.
Dunyor’s stories are most often told through the eyes of the souls, the members of
Eterion’s First March, (in)voluntary expeditioners from various planes of Dunyor
who were brought to Eterion by one of Bruma’s Purities at the moment of their
death. Their minds have been torn and they can hardly remember their past lives.
Their second chance came at a great cost, and they will be the ones to document
and shape this cruel place in hopes of repaying their debt.

sections.title: The Seasons
sections.content:
# The Seasons

<!-- chapter: 01-introduction | pages: 6-6 -->

Halice is the start of the cycle, defined
by ideals of Beauty, Freedom, Survival
and Progress. Embodied by idealists and
custodians, it seeks to preserve the good
parts of the past while violently
restructuring the bad ones. This noble
pursuit of iteration upon the familiar is,
however, easily hijacked by those who
would seek to profit from its efforts -
Survival can easily be twisted into greed,
Freedom can be taken to represent
brutal natural law.
Vamor follows once the new world order
has been established. It is represented by
the ideals of Ambition, Cunning, Passion
and Design. The pioneers and architects of Vamor aim to take advantage of this new
prosperous reality to undertake grand projects and bend the world to their will.
They believe that the wondrous and grand ends justify the often unfortunate
means. Those who would not perish for the grand project may as well be worthless.
Bruma is the inevitable realisation of what had occurred, a wholly human reaction
to the collateral damages of Vamor. It channels Altruism, Empathy, Diligence and
Safety through its folk heroes and martyrs in hopes of mending the world’s woes.
However noble its intent, Bruma’s self-destructive tendencies ultimately make it a
deeply flawed and unhealthy worldview. In the extremes, it promotes martyrdom to
the point of eating itself alive.
Trumst, armed with the knowledge of the cycle’s failed experiments, takes a final
rational approach to the issue of the human experience. Unity, Order, Curiosity and
Truth guide its rulers and peacekeepers in the creation of a fair and optimal world.
While efficient and orderly, this ideology wishes above all else to turn humans into
perfect cogs to fit its grand system, often failing to meet individual needs due to its
ruthless focus on reason. Eventually, the machine is torn down by those who would
not submit to its iron fist, and the cycle begins anew…

sections.title: Ambedo
sections.content:
# Ambedo

<!-- chapter: 01-introduction | pages: 7-7 -->

A cyan-blue matter known as ambedo populates the majority of Dunyor’s surface in
various concentrations. While some places have only faint hints of its particles, in
places with higher concentrations ambedo dust can form into ambedic crystals –
empty vessels capable of imprinting and storing human emotion and thus memory.
The study and application of this phenomena, known as ambedics, is in an ongoing
and scattered infancy, relegated to sponsored scholars and daring explorers of the
planar edges.
The simplest use of the ambedic crystals is as storage of memories. When a
sentient being experiences a particularly strong emotion near an empty crystal,
their current memories and point of view get imprinted onto the crystal and may
later be accessed in full immersion by anyone in possession of an eidoloscope, a
specialized memory delving device often employed by clairvoyants.
Alternatively, some ambedic crystals are found already filled with something
incomprehensible to an eidoloscope. These are ambedic batteries, energy vessels
with a seemingly infinite lifespan yet a strict capacity limit. Going over the limit
shatters the crystal, making it vital not to accidentally overwork whichever system
was utilizing it. Single batteries are used to power simple mechanisms or construct
drones, while multiple may be incorporated into larger machinery. These batteries
are exceedingly rare, and nobody in the public eye seems to be aware of how they
were created.
Empty crystals may also be turned into short distance wireless communication
devices via etching, enabling them to be used as relays between each other and
sentient beings. This technology powers all kinds of sophisticated prosthetics and
serves as the primary means of controlling constructs.
Finally, any ambedic crystal can simply be crushed into dust and applied as a kind of
psychological weapon. Inhaling or ingesting ambedic dust causes most humans to
enter madness, wild mood swings or a vegetative trance. Prolonged exposure may
make these effects permanent.

sections.title: What You Need
sections.content:
# What You Need

<!-- chapter: 01-introduction | pages: 8-10 -->

Narrator. A person playing as the world and all of its non-player inhabitants, the
main storyteller and the head judge of all rules. It is their duty to feed the story to
the players and to guide them on their journey. They will roleplay as various
characters and they will describe how the world reacts to the players and their
actions.
Players. The main cast of the story. Each player will take on a role of their own
character(s) and navigate the world and the story through their perspective. They
will make important decisions and will bend the world to their will through their
convictions. It is recommended that an average party consists of no more than 4
players, although more could be had with some difficulty. The aim of this system is
to allow for meaningful roleplay, so it comes naturally that this will be better
showcased when each character has more time to shine. My personal preferred
party size is 3 players due to the asymmetry this creates in party disagreements.
This Rulebook. It contains the vast majority of what is needed to understand the
game’s mechanics and all the information a player would need to play the game.
Dice. You will need three 6-sided dice and one 20-sided die for each player. Only
one set is really required to play but it is just convenient for everyone to have their
own dice. The Narrator may benefit from having a few extra d6.
Character Sheets. The sheets showcasing the characters’ stats, either in a paper or
digital format. You will often reference these during gameplay.
The Narrator should also look into these:
Battlemaps. While playing without them is possible, battlemaps are an integral part
of the tactical combat in Reverie and are heavily recommended. If playing in person,
they can be hand drawn or printed. If playing online, a virtual tabletop is
recommended. It is always nice to have pretty battlemaps, but functional sketches
will do the job just as well. If you want a free tabletop that works great for online
play and can also be used for combat when playing in person, I recommend you
check out Owlbear Rodeo. It is what I use for my games.

Sound System. Having a way to play ambiance, music and other sound effects will
greatly enhance your players’ immersion. Depending on the group, having recurring
character themes and tone songs could greatly enhance the entire experience.
Notes. A way to take notes of what happens throughout the story is heavily
recommended.
Narrative Module. Unless the Narrator is making a completely new narrative, it is
recommended that they look into prepared stories and change them to make them
their own. For newer Narrators, this is an excellent way to get a feel for Dunyor as
modules are designed to be non-linear in how they present their situations and can
easily be modified to suit any Narrator’s authorial voice. This practice is heavily
encouraged for those familiar with the system and is the biggest strength of the
TTRPG medium.

What you should read as a player
As a player, you need to be aware of Reverie’s basic mechanics, have a rough idea of
what different character progression options exist, and have a very limited
knowledge of the available items, mostly concerning your own character.
Those unfamiliar with the system’s basics should fully read chapters 1-3 as they
explain all of the basic mechanics to a satisfactory degree.
Those who are ready to make their own character should fully read chapter 4 as
well as skim over chapters 5-7. Chapter 5 contains a catalogue of classes, chapter 6
a catalogue of disciplines and abilities while chapter 7 contains the catalogue of all
aspects. These comprise the majority of what makes a character unique, and should
be read with the goal of finding interesting features for your character.
Finally, chapter 8 contains detailed lists of items and explains some additional item
mechanics like crafting and brewing. You don’t need to read through all of that, but
you will certainly find something useful in regards to any particular character in
there, ranging from different weapon options to entire systems like piloting
constructs.
What you should read as a Narrator
Everything, though it should also be noted that you don’t really need to have an
in-depth understanding of all classes, abilities or items or memorize them by heart.
Rather, you should seek to have a full mental image of the book and the system in
order to be able to better guide your players and answer any questions they might
have.

# Playing the Game (Overview)

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 11-11 -->

CH II. Playing the Game
Before anything, we must go over the basic mechanics that you will be using the
most during gameplay. It is vital to get a decent grasp of them in order to
understand how to create characters later.

sections.title: Dice
sections.content:
# Dice

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 11-11 -->

Only two types of dice are ever used in Reverie: 6-sided (also known as “d6”) and
20-sided (“d20”). This kind of notation will be used throughout this rulebook.

sections.title: Flow of The Game
sections.content:
# Flow of The Game

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 11-11 -->

Most gameplay bits of Reverie can be described as scenes. The Narrator will
typically present the environment as well as point out a few details or points of
interest before handing off the spotlight to the players. From that point onwards,
the players will, as seems natural, interact with this scene through their characters.
They may investigate, talk to non-player characters, discuss things amongst one
another and so on.
Scenes should always have a goal of some kind, be it a piece of exposition or
character building, an opportunity to gain some kind of advantage or item, a
combat encounter or anything else that would make sense in the story. When the
goal of the scene is reached, the Narrator should transition the game to a new one.
Whenever a player character attempts to do something uncertain or even remotely
difficult, the Narrator should present the character with a skill check of an
appropriate challenge level. This will be explained in the next section.
Whenever the Narrator or a player encounters a situation where they aren’t certain
of what should happen or what to decide, they may make a destiny roll. To do so,
they determine two or more possible options and assign them to the numbers or
ranges of a d20 die and roll it. This random number generator is a simple way for
Narrators to introduce volatility to scenes and a useful way to resolve potential
decision uncertainties for players.

sections.title: Skill Checks
sections.content:
# Skill Checks

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 12-13 -->

When playing the game, you will often be faced with tasks that require a specific
skill set to be completed. In these instances, you will perform a skill check. Each
skill check will consist of rolling 3d6, adding them up and then further adding the
values of a relevant skill your character possesses, as determined by the Narrator.
For each rank you have in the required attribute and skill you will add +1 to the final
result. If the final result matches or exceeds the assigned challenge level (CL) you
will have succeeded the skill check.
Radiant Success
When performing a skill check, a radiant success is achieved when the result of a
roll is higher than the required CL by at least 4. When you achieve a radiant
success, your character will perform the task with exceptional ease, inspiring hope
and restoring 3 Vigor or 3 Strain as chosen by the player.
Narrative Failure
Since Reverie is a system with binary success/failure on rolls, it is important to
ensure the players are never just told that “nothing happens” after a failure. It is the
duty of the Narrator to attempt to provide the players with new rolls, situations and
complications if they fail instead of completely cutting off the game’s narrative.

assigned by the Narrator. It ranges from 3 to 22 and must be met or exceeded by
any given roll in order for it to be successful. The table below should serve as a soft
guide to Narrators for assigning a CL of a task. Keep in mind that tasks with a CL

sections.title: Attributes
sections.content:
# Attributes

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 14-14 -->

Attributes are the main bodily properties of each creature that serve as limitations
of their skills. There are 4 different attributes:
● Grit: Your physical body. The resilience and power of flesh and bone.
● Reflex: Your uncontrolled impulses. The precise senses and natural instincts.
● Intellect: Your pointed mind. The library of knowledge and its application.
● Psyche: Your own soul. The internal will and the poetry to communicate it.
These attributes will be abbreviated to GRT, REF, INT and PSY. These colors will
also be used to represent the attributes in related concepts like skills.
Attributes each have 4 available ranks, each rank being achieved by investing a
single attribute point into it and raising the maximum rank skills under it can be
upgraded to by 2. The starting rank of each attribute is 1.
Attributes are important as they serve as a requirement for skill advancement as
well as necessary prerequisites for handling certain items and equipment. They are
much harder to improve than your skills, so be deliberate with investing into them.

sections.title: Core Skills
sections.content:
# Core Skills

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 15-15 -->

Each character has access to a total of 12 unique core skills, 3 nested in each of the
attributes. They have a total of 8 ranks which each represent +1 added to the result
when used to perform a roll. These skills represent the learned capability to
perform specific actions within the world.
To increase the rank of a skill the character has to spend 1/1/2/2/3/3/4/4
experience points. Skills may be increased at any point during downtime as long as
the character has enough xp. The full list of core skills includes:
GRT:
Athletics - Raw physicality. Your ability to influence the world with your body’s
power.
Brawling - Hand-to-hand combat. Your unarmed combat prowess and the ability to
intimidate others.
Endurance - Bodily resilience. Your ability to withstand pain and various harsh
conditions.
REF:
Dexterity - Balance and coordination. Your ability to perform elegant and acrobatic
movements.
Perception - The senses. Your ability to detect things in your surroundings.
Stealth - Elusiveness. Your ability to hide from others and pass unnoticed.
INT:
Knowledge - The encyclopedia of facts. Your ability to recall basic information
about the world.
Reasoning - Critical thinking. Your ability to apply logic and notice patterns.
Survival - Bodily familiarity. Your ability to perform first aid and take care of your
needs.
PSY:
Intuition - Empathy. Your ability to sense the motivations of others.
Persuasion - Charm. your ability to negotiate and barter.
Willpower - Mental resilience. Your ability to resist the will of others.

sections.title: Special Skills
sections.content:
# Special Skills

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 16-16 -->

Special skills are a set of 12 additional, more narrow skills that can be chosen by
individual characters who would benefit from having them. Each character may
take on up to 5 special skills in addition to core skills. Special skills can increase in
rank in the same way as core skills. They include:
GRT:
Carry - Back strength. Your ability to carry heavy items and armour over a
prolonged period.
Discipline - Nerve and courage. Your ability to maintain a clear mind under physical
pressure and duress.
Stance - Posture. your ability to grip items and avoid tripping.
REF:
Interface - Sleight of hand. Your ability to perform precise hand movements like
lockpicking.
Pilot - Systemic coordination. Your ability to operate vehicles and siege weapons.
Scout - Worldly navigation. Your ability to survey and quickly traverse areas.
INT:
Engineering - Advanced problem solving. Your ability to apply scientific principles
to complex tasks and craft items.
Lore - Studied narratives. Your knowledge of the world’s history, geography and the
humanities.
Medicine - Anatomy and herbalism. Your ability to mend injuries and brew
concoctions.
PSY:
Authority - Soft force. Your ability to impose your will onto others.
Deception - Dishonesty and composure. Your ability to lie and manipulate others.
Whisper - Planar entanglement. Your ability to interact with non-humans and the
unknowable.

sections.title: Collaborations
sections.content:
# Collaborations

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 17-17 -->

Collaborations are skill checks that involve multiple people all participating at the
same time. Their individual tasks may all be the same, for example, when opening a
heavy door, or different, like when assisting a medical operation.
In those situations, the average CL of the grand task should be chosen and then
multiplied for each participant. When making the skill rolls, the scores of the
participants are pooled together and compared against the multiplied CL.

sections.title: Contested Rolls
sections.content:
# Contested Rolls

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 17-18 -->

When a skill check would act in direct conflict with another character, it is called a
contested roll. In contested rolls there usually isn’t a set CL.
Let’s take an attempt to sneak by a guard with the Stealth skill as an example:
The person attempting to sneak by using Stealth will have to make a roll against the
guard who is using their Perception skill. They will both roll their respective skill
checks and those results will be compared.
If the Stealth roll result is strictly higher than the Perception roll result, the
character successfully sneaks by. However, should the roll be a tie or should the
Stealth roll achieve a lesser result than that of the Perception roll, The guard will
spot the character.
In contested rolls there is an active side (the one initiating the situation) and a
passive side. The active side needs to score higher than the passive side to win.
Ties are counted in the passive side’s favor.
Some examples of common contested skill matchups may include:
● Perception vs Stealth
● Persuasion vs Willpower
● Deception vs Intuition
● Athletics vs Athletics
● …
Sometimes, the Narrator may decide that a contested roll is a waste of time and
may provide a static CL instead of rolling for the defender. In those situations it is

important to keep in mind that this is still a contested roll and that a tie results in a
victory for the passive side.
In some situations there might not be an apparent passive side. When the rolls
result in a tie in those situations, just repeat the roll until it is no longer a tie.

sections.title: Exert
sections.content:
# Exert

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 18-18 -->

After performing any kind of roll, a player unsatisfied with the result may attempt
to push their character beyond their regular limits, exerting the roll.
In doing so, the character will suffer strain equal to 25% of their strain limit,
rounded up. The player may choose any die from the exerted roll and reroll it.
Exerting is not limited by anything but the character’s capacity for strain and can
be repeated as many times as wanted as long as the excess strain doesn’t kill the
character.

Exerting is not limited by anything but the character’s capacity for strain and can be repeated as many times as wanted as long as the excess strain doesn’t kill the character.

sections.title: Advantage and Disadvantage
sections.content:
# Advantage and Disadvantage

<!-- chapter: 02-playing-the-game | pages: 18-18 -->

When rolling with advantage, you may reroll the lowest die and keep the higher
score of the two. The opposite is true for rolling with disadvantage, where you keep
the lower of the two results.
These terms will sometimes come up in various abilities.

sections.title: Survival and Combat (Overview)
sections.content:
# Survival and Combat (Overview)

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 19-19 -->

CH III. Survival and Combat
Dangerous situations like combat have additional systems in order to be precisely
handled. Combat itself can come in many forms, be it a short duel, a skirmish, a
vehicular engagement or even an entire army battle or siege. A large portion of the
rulebook and the character sheet is dedicated to these situations and gameplay
loops and they are an integral part of the game.

sections.title: Vigor
sections.content:
# Vigor

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 19-20 -->

Vigor (VG) is a measure of a character’s resistance to harm and health. It is lost
when the character receives damage (DMG), be it in combat or otherwise. Every
character starts with a vigor limit (VL) of 5 which increases by 1 each time they
reach a new Tier. VL can be further increased by picking the relevant
Advancements when leveling up. Narratively, vigor serves to represent minor
injuries that wouldn’t significantly impact the combatant’s performance.
Reaching 0 VG
The point at which a character reaches 0 VG is the first time they get properly
injured in the encounter. They finally got too tired to properly dodge or parry the
enemy’s attacks, and something hit them hard. Adrenaline is flooding their system
so they aren’t exactly sure what happened yet, but they know they must make a
choice:
● Manifest Will
● Accept Fate
● Defy Death
Manifesting your will will allow your character to perform one final action which
will automatically and critically succeed before they die. This should not be chosen
lightly.

Accepting your fate will lead to the character falling unconscious and suffering an
injury. They will wake up if a successful CL 14 survival check is performed or after
sufficiently resting. If their wounds are too severe, however, they will require
further medical aid in order to avoid death.
Defying death is a compromise in which the character exposes themselves to
further danger, risking it all, in order to complete their goal. From that point
onwards until they fall unconscious, each instance of DMG they receive can become
lethal - whenever they are damaged they roll a single d6. No skills or attributes
affect this roll. Should the result be 4 or higher, the character will tank the blow and
continue to live. Otherwise, they will be immediately struck down.
When the encounter ends, the character still sustains an injury, falls unconscious
and must then be stabilized via a survival or medicine check in order to avoid
further injuries and death.
Regaining VG
HP can be regained through multiple means. The most common is to perform a
rest, but it can also be achieved through some consumables and even some
abilities.
Enemy VG
To further elaborate on the nature of VG, we should explain how enemy VG should
be interpreted. Just like your own, their VG is a measure of how much damage they
can take without taking a hit to combat performance. Reducing their VG to 0 opens
them up for you to exact your will upon them, be it by inflicting a debilitating injury
or executing them on the spot. Keep in mind that some determined or powerful
enemies might have abilities that allow them to evade such a fate in a similar way to
player characters.

sections.title: Injuries
sections.content:
# Injuries

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 20-21 -->

Mentioned previously as a consequence of reaching 0 VG, injuries are exactly what
they sound like. They inflict a constant penalty to specific rolls which would use the
affected body part, and they take a long time to heal. To determine what kind of
injury a character will get upon being knocked out, we consider multiple factors.
Keep in mind that these should be looked at after the encounter has ended.

Injury Severity
Severity is determined by the VG the character has at the end of the encounter. For
every 2 points of VG below 1, the severity increases by 1. For example, a character
who collapsed at 0 or -1 VG will only sustain an injury with the severity of 1,
whereas a character who collapsed at -4 VG will sustain an injury with the severity
of 3.
Injury Penalties
An injury is to be inflicted to a part of the body that is determined by the Narrator
and should preferably align with the method used to inflict it. The penalties of an
injury are always the same:
You gain -X on all rolls that would utilize the injured part of your body where X is the
severity of the injury.
Healing Injuries
Healing happens passively while the character is not performing any demanding
task over long periods of time. By default, it takes 4 weeks to reduce the severity of
an injury by 1.
First Aid
First aid is performed upon combat end and is crucial in making sure the recovery
goes smoothly. First aid can be given by any character by performing a survival or
Medicine skill check with the CL of [ 12 + Severity ]. If successful, the injury will
take significantly shorter to fully heal. If survival was used, each point of severity
will take only 3 weeks to heal. If medicine was used, each point of severity will take
only 2 weeks to heal.

sections.title: Strain
sections.content:
# Strain

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 22-22 -->

Strain (SN) is a measure of your character’s morale and exhaustion. Strain increases
whenever a character performs advanced abilities, exhausting activities or gets
otherwise demoralized or tired. Every character starts with a strain limit (SL) of 5
which increases by 1 each time they reach a new Tier. SL can be further increased
by picking the relevant advancements when leveling up. Strain is also important for
a number of different character centered systems that will be discussed in later
chapters.
Suffering Strain in Combat
Whenever your character would reach 0 or less VG, they gain SN equal to half of
their maximum SL. This can only occur once per combat encounter.
Getting Rid of Strain
There are plenty of ways to remove a character’s Strain. The most common is
through resting, but a variety of consumables and a fair number of abilities also
offer strain restoration. In addition to those, the Narrator may also determine some
strain should be lost during moments of hope and overall positive events. Examples
of such events may include:
-1 SN: succeeding an important skill check, reaching a beautiful view
-2 SN: surviving a tough encounter, reaching safe shelter
-3 SN: succeeding on a CL 18 or tougher roll,
Standing On The Edge
Should a character’s SN ever increase past their SL, their mind will be put to test
and they will have to pass a CL 18 conviction check (3d6 + chosen conviction) in
order not to suffer a crisis. Convictions and crises are fully explained in chapter 4.
Diving Into The Abyss
Should your character ever reach double their SL, they will suffer a heart attack and
be reduced to [ 1 + Endurance ] of their maximum HP and their SN will be reset
back to the maximum SL. The second heart attack will always be lethal. Should a
character wish to avoid the risk of the second heart attack, they can choose to
Accept Fate upon reaching the first one.

sections.title: Combat Encounters
sections.content:
# Combat Encounters

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 23-23 -->

Combat encounters are more rigid than other parts of gameplay as they aim to
more rigidly simulate the events of the scene. In them, characters use their
equipment and abilities in tactical gameplay in order to incapacitate their enemies
or achieve another goal. They feature a defined timeline and turn order as well as
rules for how much time actions take to perform. Combat encounters involving
more than a couple of characters should be played out on a square grid in order to
make them simpler to follow.
Turn Order
Who goes first in an encounter should be determined by simple reasoning or
agreed upon by the players if they are going first. You could say the character with
the highest REF would go first, or you could say it would be the character who
threw the first punch in a brawl, or anything else that makes sense for that
situation.
After the first character finishes their turn, a character from the opposing side of
the conflict, your enemy, is given a turn in the same way as determined by the
Narrator. The combat round consists of a constant exchange of allied and enemy
character turns until all present characters have played out their turns. If there are
more enemies than allies or vice versa, the side with more characters gets to play
out their remaining turns in sequence after the side with less characters is fully
finished for the round.
Rounds and Turns
Combat in Reverie happens in rounds where each combatant gets a turn to
perform their actions. Take note of this distinction as it is important for some
effects and abilities.
Your Options
During a single combat round, each player characters and most humanoid
non-player characters has:
● 1 Movement Action to use during their turn
● 3 Action Points (ACP) to spend on abilities during their turn
● 1 Reaction that can be used at any point in the round
sections.searchText: Combat Encounters Combat encounters are more rigid than other parts of gameplay as they aim to more rigidly simulate the events of the scene. In them, characters use their equipment and abilities in tactical gameplay in order to incapacitate their enemies or achieve another goal. They feature a defined timeline and turn order as well as rules for how much time actions take to perform. Combat encounters involving more than a couple of characters should be played out on a square grid in order to make them simpler to follow. Turn Order Who goes first in an encounter should be determined by simple reasoning or agreed upon by the players if they are going first. You could say the character with the highest REF would go first, or you could say it would be the character who threw the first punch in a brawl, or anything else that makes sense for that situation. After the first character finishes their turn, a character from the opposing side of the conflict, your enemy, is given a turn in the same way as determined by the Narrator. The combat round consists of a constant exchange of allied and enemy character turns until all present characters have played out their turns. If there are more enemies than allies or vice versa, the side with more characters gets to play out their remaining turns in sequence after the side with less characters is fully finished for the round. sections.title: Movement
sections.content:
# Movement

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 24-24 -->

On each of their turns, each combatant gets a movement action. On a movement
action, a character can elect to move in any direction for as much as their speed
allows. A character’s speed is calculated using the following formula:
Movement Speed
[ Athletics + GRT + REF ]
To find out how many tiles a character can travel in a single movement action,
compare their Movement Speed value to the information below:
0-1: 2 tiles
2-4: 3 tiles
5-9: 4 tiles
10+: 5 tiles
Tile conversion
Tiles can be directly translated into real measurements:
1 tile = 1.5m ~ 5 feet
For the sake of simplicity, this rulebook will only express combat distances in tiles.

sections.title: Abilities (Base Actions)
sections.content:
# Abilities (Base Actions)

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 24-25 -->

Abilities
Most actions you can perform in combat in Reverie are abilities. They have
specified costs, requirements and effects. You will learn more about specific
abilities in the sections regarding different disciplines - collections of abilities that
encompass different styles of combat. The amount of ACP an ability costs is
dependant on its speed, which can be either of the following:
[ >>> ] Slow (3 action points)
[ >> ] Average (2 action points)
[ > ] Swift (1 action point)
[ I ] Instant (0 action points)
[ < ] Reaction (1 reaction)
Stronger and more impactful abilities tend to require more ACP as well as more
strain.

While different characters may have varying abilities depending on their class,
disciplines or equipment, all characters always have access to this set of 7 basic
abilities:
>> Cautious Attack
Melee/Ranged Attack
Requirements: none
| 0 SN | +1 ACC | -1 DMG |
Effect:
-
>> Reckless Attack
Melee/Ranged Attack
Requirements: none
| 0 SN | -1 ACC | +1 DMG |
Effect:
-
>> Dodge
Defensive
Requirements: none
| 0 SN | +0 EVA |
Effect:
Gain EVA equal to your Dexterity/2,
rounded down, until the end of your
turn.
>> Brace
Defensive
Requirements: none
| 0 SN | +0 EVA |
Effect:
Your armour points are increased by
your Endurance/2, rounded down,
until the end of your turn.
>> Reload/Switch
Defensive
Requirements: none
| 0 SN | +0 EVA |
Effect:
Reload your currently equipped
weapon, switch your equipped weapon
or pick up an object from the ground.
> Interact/Consumable
Utility
Requirements: none
| 0 SN |
Effect:
Perform a skill check while interacting
with the environment or use a
consumable item on yourself or an
adjacent target.
> Dash
Utility
Requirements: none
| 1 SN |

Gain an additional movement action.

sections.title: The Combat Roll
sections.content:
# The Combat Roll

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 26-27 -->

Whenever any kind of attack ability is performed, a combat roll is made to
determine its success, not unlike a skill check that is usually used to perform
non-combat tasks. Combat rolls do not use skills or attributes, but some weapons
have attribute requirements in order to be used effectively.
Each combat roll will include 3d6, your character’s Class rank and any additional
modifiers the ability you are performing may provide.
Combat Roll
[ 3d6 + Class Rank + MOD ]
The attribute relevant to the weapon is different for each unique weapon and listed
in its stats. Combat rolls are not rolled against a set CL but rather the target’s
evasion.
Accuracy
Accuracy (ACC) is the most common modifier that can affect a combat roll. It is
gained or lost depending on the effects of each ability. Each point of accuracy
represents +1 that is added to the combat roll.
Damage
Damage (DMG) represents harm. Most attacks tend to deal some, and taking
damage is reflected in losing HP should it not be stopped by armour or some other
means.

Evasion
Evasion (EVA) is a measure of a character’s ability to defend themselves in combat,
be it by dodging or parrying attacks. Its purpose is to avoid DMG and it acts as the
first layer of defense against all attacks - it is the CL that all attacks targeting the
character roll against. Its value starts at 10 for regular characters and can be further
increased through gear and abilities.
Armour
Whenever a character would take DMG, if they are wearing armour or have
otherwise obtained armour points (AP) in some way, the DMG is reduced by their
AP. Armour points act as a form of permanent damage reduction but they can be
depleted through the use of abilities. Depleted AP are restored at the end of a
combat encounter.
Armour is split into light, medium and heavy categories. The categories, while
generally defining the armour’s effectiveness, also have unique requirements to be
worn and associated downsides:
● Light Armour: no requirements, no penalties
● Medium Armour: Carry 3, disadvantage on Stealth checks
● Heavy Armour: Carry 6, disadvantage on Stealth checks and -1 tile movement
Characters who are wearing a piece of armour without meeting the Carry skill
requirement receive a -2 penalty to combat rolls and a -1 tile movement penalty.
Damage Overflow
When a character successfully performs an attack, depending on their roll they may
inflict additional DMG depending on its result. For each 2 points the roll achieved
over the target EVA, +1 DMG is added to the attack. This represents the fact that
more accurate strikes are obviously going to hurt more. For example, an attack that
rolls 12 against a target with 10 EVA will deal +1 DMG, while an attack that rolls 16
against a target with 11 EVA will deal +2 DMG. These bonuses are added to the
weapon’s base damage value to achieve a final DMG of the attack.

sections.title: Abilities In Detail
sections.content:
# Abilities In Detail

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 28-28 -->

Now that the combat roll and basic combat terms have been covered, we can take a
better look at abilities and how they should be read. The symbol in the top left
describes the amount of ACP required to perform it and the color of the symbol
describes its type (attack/defensive/utility). Below that, there is the ability subtype
that further signifies the specifics of using this ability (for example a “1H Melee
Attack” is an attack ability that can only be performed with one-handed melee
weapons. Specific requirements are listed in the row after that one. The stats line
always covers the SN cost of using the ability while attacks go on to describe the
ACC and DMG modifiers of the attack while defensive abilities modify EVA. Finally,
the effect describes any specific effects of the ability that have not yet been
covered.
>> Reckless Attack —> Ability speed (ACP cost), type and name
Melee/Ranged Attack —> Ability subtypes
Requirements: none —> Weapon type/other requirements
| 0 SN | -1 ACC | +1 DMG | —> SN cost and ACC/DMG/EVA modifiers
Effect: —> Unique effects
-
Each character always has access to all of the basic abilities and abilities provided
to them by their class. In addition, characters get to have 6 active abilities from any
of the discipline abilities they know. Using inactive but known abilities costs a
destiny point. It is important to note that no ability may be performed more than
once per combat round unless stated otherwise in its effect.
Capstone Abilities
Characters may also cast abilities from their adopted disciplines that are a rank
above their current access. Doing so costs 1 destiny point. This is meant to allow for
the players to test out new abilities before learning them as well as provide
expensive power spikes in dire situations

sections.title: Melee Combat
sections.content:
# Melee Combat

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 29-29 -->

When engaged in melee combat, to perform attacks combatants must be within the
effective range of their weapons which is Adjacent by default but can be modified
through the use of abilities.
Flanking
If a character is engaged in melee combat with multiple opponents all of their
enemies gain +1 ACC on attacks targeting the flanked character per enemy engaged
beyond the first. The maximum value this bonus can reach is +4. For example, two
bandits fighting against a player character would each receive +1 ACC to their rolls.
Using Both Hands
If a character’s weapon doesn’t take up two hands already, they gain the ability to
pick up an offhand to complement their main weapon.
Any one-handed melee weapon can be used as an offhand, providing +1 EVA to the
character using it and allowing them to also perform abilities that would require it.
Shields
Shields, with exceptions, focus on predictable defense, offering an additional way to
gain AP. They are an excellent choice for a sidearm if you require reliable
survivability.
Other Options
There also exists a wide variety of tools and combat items that can come in handy
in a combat encounter like pistols, hooks, bombs and so on. Keep in mind that you
might also sometimes want a free hand in order to interact with the environment.

sections.title: Ranged Combat
sections.content:
# Ranged Combat

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 30-30 -->

In ranged combat further modifiers are often applied to your combat rolls
depending on the target’s position:
Distance:
Too close: -3 ACC
Effective range: +0 ACC
Too far: -2 ACC
Target Cover:
No cover: +0 ACC
Half cover: -1 ACC
¾ cover: -2 ACC
Full cover: -3 ACC
Speed:
Stationary: +0 ACC
Fast (speed above 4 tiles/round): -1 ACC
Incredibly fast (e.g. dragon): -3 ACC
Range Zones
All weapons have their effective range zones which are described as:
Adjacent (1 tile)
Close (2-3 tiles)
Medium (4-7 tiles)
Long (8-12 tiles)
Very Long (13+ tiles)
For one-handed thrown weapons, assume the optimal ranges to be Close and
Medium unless stated otherwise. For two-handed weapons, assume it to be just
Close.

sections.title: Burden
sections.content:
# Burden

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 31-31 -->

Burden is a measure of how cumbersome it is to function while carrying items. The
burden value of different items is listed in their stats. The intent behind this
mechanic is not to force you to meticulously track your inventory but rather to
limit your actual combat loadout to something reasonable. Burden can largely be
ignored in situations where your character is not in a time sensitive or dangerous
scene or doesn’t explicitly need to always carry all of their items. The maximum
burden a character can carry is determined by the following formula:
Burden
[ 6+GRT+Endurance+2*Carry ]
Beyond this threshold, the character suffers -1 on all rolls that use GRT or REF and
all combat rolls for every point of burden above it.
Should a character reach -10 on rolls via burden penalties, they can no longer move.
Armour Burden
The burden of worn armour is reduced by 1 for each rank the character has in the
carry skill. This is only applied while the armour is worn.
The Purpose of Burden
Burden should not be something you have to manage often, it should be there to
make you consider what weapons, armour and equipment you are carrying into
combat. This makes burden act not as a real penalty, but rather as a loadout limiter,
punishing you only if you can’t decide what you should be carrying around.

sections.title: Status Effects and Conditions
sections.content:
# Status Effects and Conditions

<!-- chapter: 03-survival-and-combat | pages: 32-33 -->

Certain attacks and abilities can sometimes have unique or lasting effects on their
targets. Instead of repeating longer rules for these conditions, they are instead
explained here and given a keyword that actually appears in ability texts.
Pierce X - The attack inflicting this effect applies to bypasses up to X points of
armour on a successful hit.
Break X - The attack inflicting this effect depletes X points of armour on a
successful hit.
Stun X - Afflicted creature has -X on combat rolls. The level of the effect is reduced
by one at the end of the creature’s turn and by two upon performing a defensive
action.
Bleeding X - Afflicted creature loses X vigor at the beginning of its combat turn or
once every minute. The effect can be reduced by 1 by performing a defensive action
or by 2 by spending 2 AP to perform a successful survival skill check with a CL equal
to 12+X. Creatures wearing unbroken medium or heavy armour or using an
unbroken shield are immune to bleeding.
Burn X - Afflicted creature loses X vigor at the beginning of its turn. The level of
the effect is reduced by one when it damages the afflicted creature and by two
upon performing a defensive action. Burn deals +2 DMG to targets without armour.
Soulburn X - Afflicted creature loses X vigor at the beginning of its turn. The level
of the effect is reduced by two upon performing a defensive action. Upon reaching
0 VG, soulburn is cleansed and Burn 1 is applied.
X Temporary Vigor (TMV) - Afflicted creature has X additional vigor unaffected by
armour that is depleted before the main health pool.
Fractured X - Afflicted creature’s abilities cost +1 AP to perform. The level of the
effect is reduced by 1 at the end of the afflicted creature’s turn or by 2 upon
performing a defensive action and succeeding a CL 12+X discipline skill check.
Prone - Afflicted creature loses its reaction for this turn. At the start of its next
turn, it loses 2 AP and its movement action.
Feeble X - Afflicted creature deals -X DMG during its next turn.
Blind X - Afflicted creature suffers -8 ACC on all ranged attacks and abilities during
its next X turns.
Immobilized X - Afflicted creature is unable to move during its next X turns.
Unaware - Unaware creatures have 0 EVA.

Stealth - Other creatures are Unaware of the creature that is in Stealth. This effect
is lost upon entering a creature’s line of sight or performing an attack within their
line of sight.
Taunted - Afflicted creature has -2 on all attacks not targeting the creature that
inflicted taunt during its next 2 turns.
Intimidated - Afflicted creature has -2 on all attacks targeting the creature that
inflicted taunt during its next 2 turns.
Pull X - Moves the target X tiles towards you.
Push X - Moves the target X tiles away from you.

sections.content:
# Characters in Depth (Overview)

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 34-34 -->

CH IV. Characters in Depth
This chapter covers several mechanics tied directly to characters which can make a
significant impact on how you navigate the game world and roleplay. It also
includes a guide for creating characters that extends into the next three chapters
which provide various options for character building respectively.

sections.title: What Constitutes a Character
sections.content:
# What Constitutes a Character

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 34-34 -->

Each player character and important non player character has the following
mechanical traits and stats which make them unique:
● Attributes
● Core and special skills
● Vigor, strain and evasion
● Convictions and failings
● Origin
● Tier and levels
● Class
● Disciplines
● Aspects
Out of these, all of the concepts that have not yet been explained will be introduced
in this chapter and expanded to list all of their options in the following chapters.

sections.title: Destiny Points
sections.content:
# Destiny Points

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 34-34 -->

Destiny points (DP) are an expendable resource player characters have access to
that can be used in multiple ways. The default way they can be used is to spend a
DP after performing any roll in order to add +X to that roll’s result where X is the
rank of a conviction that aligns with that roll. These effects cannot be stacked or
combined on a single roll, and if done during combat they are limited to one use per
encounter. Various abilities and aspects a character has can sometimes give them
new ways to spend destiny points.
Gaining Destiny Points
Destiny points should be gained at least at the end of every session or once during
2-3 hours of play. Beyond that, once per that same time period, they should be
earnable when a character performs an action that aligns with their convictions.
Each character starts with a 2 DP maximum.
sections.searchText: Destiny Points Destiny points (DP) are an expendable resource player characters have access to that can be used in multiple ways. The default way they can be used is to spend a DP after performing any roll in order to add +X to that roll’s result where X is the rank of a conviction that aligns with that roll. These effects cannot be stacked or combined on a single roll, and if done during combat they are limited to one use per encounter. Various abilities and aspects a character has can sometimes give them new ways to spend destiny points. Gaining Destiny Points Destiny points should be gained at least at the end of every session or once during 2-3 hours of play. Beyond that, once per that same time period, they should be earnable when a character performs an action that aligns with their convictions. Each character starts with a 2 DP maximum.

sections.title: Convictions
sections.content:
# Convictions

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 35-36 -->

Convictions are one of the integral systems of Reverie and act as a mechanical
representation of roleplay. They are ideals and rules your characters align
themselves to and follow, and sticking to them yields powerful boons while defying
them strips the characters of destiny’s favour. While being “virtues” characters
adhere to, they also act as metaphysical forces of the world and through this can
provide boons to those who follow them.
There are a total of 16 convictions, 4 representing each of Dunyor’s seasons:
Vamor - pioneers and architects
● Design - I will put the greater design above the needs of any one person.
● Ambition - I will become more than I am, whatever the cost.
● Passion - I will make any sacrifice necessary for that which I love.
● Cunning - I will use any opportunity that benefits me, without hesitation or
guilt.
Bruma - folk heroes and martyrs
● Empathy - I will treat each person with dignity, no matter their station.
● Altruism - I will sacrifice for those who need help without expecting anything
in return.
● Safety - I will ensure the well-being of myself and those close to me above all
else.
● Diligence - I will never compromise my goals by taking shortcuts.
Trumst - rulers and peacekeepers
● Unity - I will do everything in my power to prevent needless conflict.
● Truth - I will speak with integrity, holding others accountable to the same
honesty.
● Order - I will purge degeneracy and fragility.
● Curiosity - I will always pursue new knowledge.
Halice - idealists and custodians
● Beauty - I will safeguard the wonders of the world, both crafted and born of
nature.
● Freedom - I will always pursue liberty for both myself and those around me.
● Survival - I will prioritize my own success, discarding anything that
jeopardizes it.
● Progress - I will always strive for innovation and improvement of the world.

Think of convictions as oaths your characters make to themselves. Each character
starts with at least a single conviction at rank 1 and can acquire up to 3 different
convictions at the same time. For characters starting at higher levels more
Convictions at higher ranks may be appropriate. Convictions can increase in rank in
a similar way to skills - their ranks range from 1-4 (and exceptionally 5) and
increasing them requires a destiny point investment equal to the new rank.
If a character would contradict any of their convictions in a non-insignificant way
they will suffer a crisis.

sections.title: Crisis
sections.content:
# Crisis

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 36-36 -->

Mentioned in the contexts of a character reaching their SL and defying convictions,
a crisis is the mental breaking point that occurs as a consequence of intense
psychological stress.
When faced with a crisis, the character must resolve it in one of multiple ways:
● Lower the rank of the chosen/violated conviction
● Manifest/increase the rank of the failing for that conviction
● Spend your destiny point maximum
● Abandon an aspect

sections.title: Failings
sections.content:
# Failings

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 36-37 -->

Failings are the other side of the coin when it comes to convictions. They represent
negative personality traits that manifest when characters defy their convictions and
wreak havoc on their ability to make decisions.
They work almost exactly like convictions, presenting a new rule the character
must follow while punishing them with crisis should the rule be defied.
Conflicting Oaths
Should two or more convictions or failings ever come into conflict, the one with the
higher rank has higher priority and adhering to it will not result in any DP loss.
Choosing to adhere to a conviction or failing of lower rank will result in a DP loss
equal to the difference between the ranks of the stronger conviction or failing and
the one that was chosen.

Removing a Failing
There are multiple ways to go about lowering the rank of a failing:
● Pay an amount of DP equal to the rank of the associated conviction
● Lower the rank of the associated conviction by 1 if its rank is at least as high
as that of the Failing
● Spend long periods of downtime working on getting rid of a failing (4 weeks
per rank)
Which Failing do I get?
Determining which failing a character gets should be determined by the character’s
player and the Narrator. The failing should be in some way tied to the action that
caused it and the player should provide the Narrator with their input on how they
imagine their character reacting. The Narrator still has the final say on which failing
is manifested.
There are a total of 8 different failings:
● Greed - I will put my own needs and desires above those of others.
● Paranoia - I cannot entrust others with matters that affect me.
● Despair - I cannot further my own wellbeing.
● Masochism - I will put myself in harm’s way.
● Wrath - I will punish all who oppose me.
● Arrogance - I will do everything in my power to avoid humiliation.
● Apathy - I cannot consider the wellbeing and interests of others.
● Cowardice - I will do everything in my power to avoid harm.

sections.title: Origins
sections.content:
# Origins

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 38-50 -->

Origins are a summarized backstory of your character and are chosen during
character creation. They provide your character with a narrative background in the
world and start you out with relevant special skills or discounts towards learning
relevant core skills – inspirations. They are by no means a set template you should
follow during character creation, but rather a guideline and a suggestion.
Origins are split into generic origins available to all characters and plane origins
available only to characters from that plane. It wouldn’t make sense for a character
created for a campaign in Ulvandul to have a Vesperan origin without them having
lived there and then somehow travelled between planes. As the timeline of your
world progresses and interplanar travel becomes more accessible, this restriction
should be gradually lifted.
Keep in mind that generic origins tend to give you more freedom when it comes to
what bonuses they provide while the plane specific origins tend to be more narrow
and potent.
Generic Origins
Generic origins are available to all characters regardless of their home plane.
Commoner
Your comfortable everyday existence was turned on its head, and now you must
answer the call.
Inspiration: Any basic skill
Start with: Any special skill at rank 2
Merchant
Your life of travel gave you but a tiny preview of what was to come.
Inspiration: Persuasion, Knowledge
Start with: Lore 2

Warrior
Bloodspill has always been your true calling, yet you wonder if there could be a higher
purpose to your proficiency.
Inspiration: Athletics
Start with: Armour 2, Stance 2
Brigand
You have led a life of crime and violence in a cutthroat world bent on erasing you, yet
something made you question if this was truly your destiny.
Inspiration: Dexterity, Stealth
Start with: Interface 2
Scholar
You have spent countless nights obsessing over holes in history books and incomplete
maps. It is time you took the matter of truth into your own hands.
Inspiration: Knowledge
Start with: Lore 3

Eterion Origins
The city-plane of redemption promotes the values of self reflection and altruism above
all others. Its purities guide the steady wheel of technological progress that
encompasses a vast variety of professions while the various mystics and prophets
inhabit the forgotten half-space mists on the plane’s edges. Ambedic crystals saturate
the city in vignettes of lives long gone, of moments and emotions captured in time.
The reclamation of the planar edges is an ongoing yet slow process, and the city’s
population is starting to get too large to be supported by its meager resources. The
grand solution presented by the purities are the Marches, expeditions into the planar
void, hoping to send the best and brightest of Eterion to other planes and secure the
city’s future prosperity.
Seeker
You’ve escaped death elsewhere and wound up in the city of redemption. Limitless
opportunities stretch themselves out in front of you.
Inspiration: Willpower, Any basic skill
Start with: Any special skill 2
Artisan
You have spent your life as a well oiled, productive cog in the city’s machine. Can you
take control of your own fate?
Inspiration: Reasoning or Knowledge
Start with: Carry 2, Engineering 2
City Bureaucrat
There was only so much pettiness and bickering you could handle before abandoning
your political career. You’re sure there are other fields where your skills will be more
appreciated.
Inspiration: Intuition, Persuasion
Start with: Deception 2

Memorialist
You revel in the exploration of history and people’s fates. Form your thesis and share it
with the world.
Inspiration: Intuition, Perception
Start with: Lore 2
Fogborn
You’ve lived on the edge of the plane and have learned to blend in with the shadows of
reality. Your calm demeanor and mental fortitude guide you on your endless journey.
Inspiration: Survival
Start with: Whisper 2, Lore 2

Agmar Origins
Agmar’s dead, scorched surface and everthundering skies have pushed its inhabitants
to two extremes – while ground-dwellers carve out their existence in shade the
nomads rule the skies aboard airships and on dragonback. The conflict between these
two ways of life defines the lives of the plane’s people. The city folk slave away under
the rule of the sky clans’ immense fleets, hoping to develop some way to strike down
their monsters from the sky. The major nomad clans of Khurni, Galadri and Lakumi
play political games, dividing the plane as they choose and frequently clashing over
scarce resources.
Stormrider
The sky is your one true home, the thunder your hymn. Wherever the storm takes you
next, you will accept it with an open heart and mind.
Inspiration: Survival, Dexterity
Start with: Pilot 2
Ravineborn
You have toiled day and night to carve out your existence in the harshest of climates.
You will outlast whatever storm attempts to wash over you, be it man, lizard or
thunder.
Inspiration: Endurance, Willpower
Start with: Carry 2
Sky Raider
To you, freedom doesn’t stop where another’s ends. Your countless victims were free to
resist you, you were free to pilfer them, and your desire for freedom won out.
Inspiration: Brawling
Start with: Stance 2, Pilot 2
Wastelander
Most would think you mad for choosing to live in the various crevices and tunnels of
the agmarian wastelands. Maybe they’re right, but at least your torturous existence
has taught you a trick or two about surviving in places where it shouldn’t be possible.
Inspiration: Survival, Endurance
Start with: Carry 2

Steam Artificer
You have studied long and hard to end up at the forefront of innovation. Your
knowledge of airships, thermal energy and steam engines is rivaled by none.
Inspiration: Reason
Start with: Engineering 2, Lore 2

Vesperik Origins
Vesperik’s long nights and harsh forested wilderness present a constant existential
threat to its inhabitants. Unity and order serve as the guiding light in the darkness
and most of its inhabitants have their roots in various military branches and
expeditionary forces. The Pyrex rules over a technocratic collective of guild-houses
who extend the influence of the grand city of Feulum into the untamed wilderness and
distant colonial provinces. The plane-spanning hive forest Beothran acts as a grand,
almost divine, but indifferent consciousness, spreading its influence throughout its
inhabitants, holding a grudge for each and every wound and scar the survivors dare
to inflict upon it.
Woodlands Survivor
The vast forest has been your home and prison. You are quick and quiet, for you know
what’s lurking in the dark.
Inspiration: Perception, Survival
Start with: Whisper 2
Borderlands Settler
You have carved out a bleak existence from amongst the thick black roots. Few would
survive the hardship you have endured.
Inspiration: Athletics, Willpower
Start with: Carry 2
Garrison Guard
You have dedicated yourself to the protection of humanity. You live to serve it until
your dying breath.
Inspiration: Brawling, Intuition
Start with: Authority 2
Scorchblade
You have pledged your existence to the bladed beacon. Brave the wilderness for a while
longer - the night will be over soon!
Inspiration: Endurance
Start with: Discipline 2, All tier 0 and 1 abilities from Duel.

Academa
You have learned about the world’s unending horrors from the comfort of the capital’s
walls. Guide your protectors into a better future.
Inspiration: Knowledge, Reason
Start with: Engineering 3 or Lore 3 or Medicine 3

Duiber Origins
While the evergreen plane might seem like a chilly paradise to outsiders, its
inhabitants often prove just how ruthless it can be. The mountain valleys have
produced countless isolated and strange cultures hostile to all who would intrude
upon them, and the Lords of the Valley rule over most of the plane’s interior with a
strict regime of occult collectivism. The Valley civilizations, “vallents”, heavily
subscribe to the idea of dualism, splitting both rule and society between the material
and spiritual roles. The coastfolk live bitter lives ravaged by flash-blizzards,
abandoned by their valley kin. Inside of the deep forests, the mystic followers of the
First Circle live in solitude, preparing for an unknown eternal ritual.
Coaster
The harsh eastern coasts bring naught but salt and cold wind, trapping you in
between the void and the realm of the Valley lords. Can you reclaim your existence
from these overwhelming forces?
Inspiration: Survival
Start with: Pilot 2, Carry 2
Vallentian
The valley’s splendor is unmatched by any other piece of the plane and it has allowed
you to enjoy a life of prosperity and calm in your tight-knit community. What could
have possibly led you to abandon it?
Inspiration: Intuition, Knowledge
Start with: Lore 2
Sectarian
You have both struggled and enjoyed your life in some far-removed forested glade. In
your habitat you are the perfect creature, yet a taste of the wider world is sure to clash
against your ingrained state of mind.
Inspiration: Stealth
Start with: Scout 2, Whisper 2

Circle Apostle
You have dedicated yourself to the true preservers of Halice. If anyone can mend this
broken world, it surely must be the wise circles of Duiber’s witches. You are sure that
no sacrifice could be too high to achieve this noble goal.
Inspiration: Perception
Start with: Lore 2, Medicine 2
Eye of The Lords
You have abandoned the simple life for the opportunity to serve the Lords of the Valley.
You are their eyes and claws, you are feared and respected, yet the idea that nobody
will mourn you still hasn’t left your mind.
Inspiration: Reasoning, Stealth
Start with: Authority 2

Lior Origins
Lioran deserts are soaked in the blood and sweat of those warring under the banners
of ancient clans and upstart warlords. The ancient buried cities tempt the desert’s
inhabitants with promises of old world technology and untold riches. Blood pacts are a
common custom and kin are often treated as mere currency for those unable to hold
their own. Slaver guilds scavenge the war-torn regions in search of able bodies to
excavate ancient relics. Vamor reigns supreme, enforcing ambition through blade and
bullet alike.
Tunnel Rat
You were taken by slaver companies as a child and have spent your formative years
digging through the perilous ruins in search of riches, and now freedom.
Inspiration: Dexterity, Survival
Start with: Interface 2
Clansman
You owe your life to your family and they owe their lives to you. This unbreakable
bond has been the only thing keeping you sane in these hostile deserts.
Inspiration: Intuition, Knowledge
Start with: Authority 2
Desert Skirmisher
Your life has been nothing but spilled blood and the smell of black powder. Pulling the
trigger comes to you as naturally as walking. You’ve been called heartless and cruel,
but it’s been a long time since that hatred got to you. Such are the simple ways of Lior.
Inspiration: Perception
Start with: Scout 2, All tier 0 and 1 abilities from Precision.
Reformationist
You see yourself and your city-dwelling kin as above the petty conflicts of the sands.
You have a grand vision for the future and no mercy for those who would impede it.
Inspiration: Reasoning, Willpower
Start with: Lore 2

Herd Nomad
War is the place where you and your kind are not. You’ve lived your life in the
company of the wind and the sand, refusing to partake in the widespread bloodshed.
Inspiration: Knowledge, Survival
Start with: Whisper 2

Ulvandul and Ravina origins will be added when the occasion calls.

Tunnel Rat You were taken by slaver companies as a child and have spent your formative years digging through the perilous ruins in search of riches, and now freedom. Inspiration: Dexterity, Survival Start with: Interface 2 Clansman You owe your life to your family and they owe their lives to you. This unbreakable bond has been the only thing keeping you sane in these hostile deserts. Inspiration: Intuition, Knowledge Start with: Authority 2 Desert Skirmisher Your life has been nothing but spilled blood and the smell of black powder. Pulling the trigger comes to you as naturally as walking. You’ve been called heartless and cruel, but it’s been a long time since that hatred got to you. Such are the simple ways of Lior. Inspiration: Perception Start with: Scout 2, All tier 0 and 1 abilities from Precision. Reformationist You see yourself and your city-dwelling kin as above the petty conflicts of the sands. You have a grand vision for the future and no mercy for those who would impede it. Inspiration: Reasoning, Willpower Start with: Lore 2 Herd Nomad War is the place where you and your kind are not. You’ve lived your life in the company of the wind and the sand, refusing to partake in the widespread bloodshed. Inspiration: Knowledge, Survival Start with: Whisper 2 Ulvandul and Ravina origins will be added when the occasion calls.

sections.title: Levels and Tiers
sections.content:
# Levels and Tiers

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 51-52 -->

Levels
Levels are a representation of life experience of a character, increasing by 1 for
every 5 points of experience the character has. Unlike in many other TTRPGs, in
Reverie it is rarely recommended that you start out at level 1. Levels in this game
scale linearly and starting at a very low level will restrict your progression by a
decent amount until you reach higher levels. While this is a good representation of
common people, such individuals can scarcely survive the more dangerous parts of
Dunyor. Keep in mind that levels are not arbitrary power ups but a timeline of
growth.
Tiers
Tiers are broad groupings of levels that describe the general amount of experience
a character has. They are useful when it comes to quickly determining the power
level of creatures and characters as well as solid guidelines for start and end points
of a campaign. The tiers are as following:
Tier 1 (levels 1-4) - Nobody
Attribute Rank Limit: 2
Skill Rank Limit: 2
This tier represents the faceless masses. The world will not be kind to you.
Tier 2 (levels 5-8) - Promising Soul
Attribute Rank Limit: 2
Skill Rank Limit: 3
This tier is the earliest recommended starting point for a character. These
characters are a great starting point for longer campaigns or more horror-oriented
narratives, being mostly average with a few specific areas where they can shine.
Tier 3 (levels 9-12) - Competent Individual
Attribute Rank Limit: 3
Skill Rank Limit: 3
This tier is the best starting point for starting in the middle of action. Tier 3
characters are still frail but they have begun to access tools that can turn the tides
in their favour.

Tier 4 (levels 13-16) - Skilled Professional
Attribute Rank Limit: 3
Skill Rank Limit: 4
This tier is best used for one-shots and shorter adventures. Characters are
generally competent in most areas and a balanced party can really go a long way.
These characters will rarely just fail because they are incompetent and will instead
begin to fail when they cannot bring themselves to sacrifice an important part of
themselves.
Tier 5 (levels 17-20) - Renowned Veteran
Attribute Rank Limit: 4
Skill Rank Limit: 4
This tier represents a significant milestone for lesser characters. Tier 5 characters
are well rounded and often exceptional individuals in their chosen areas of
development.
Tier 6 (levels 21-24) - Legendary Hero
This is the first endgame tier. These characters are world class in what they do and
their presence is fitting in the highest stakes adventures. They tend to either be
known far and wide or so secretive as to not be recognized by anyone but a select
few individuals.
Is there more?
You could theoretically go up in levels and tiers as much as you wanted. These later
tiers are not defined as their progression structure is identical. It is generally not
recommended to go that high in levels as characters tend to fill out all of their
weaknesses and become too well-rounded to be interesting. Tier 6 characters
should have already reached the peak of what is possible and done everything there
was to do for their world. Tier 7 characters should be dead.

sections.title: Progression and Advancements
sections.content:
# Progression and Advancements

<!-- chapter: 04-characters-in-depth | pages: 53-53 -->

Progression
Characters in Reverie have multiple improvement tracks with varying speeds:
Experience Points
Experience points (XP) are the main metric of progression, serving as a currency to
improve core and special skills of a character. XP does not have a set rate at which
it should be earned, rather the rate should be set by the Narrator for the intended
campaign length. Gaining XP also eventually leads to level increases and then to tier
increases.
Leveling Up
Upon reaching a new level characters gain the ability to pick out two
advancements from the list of available advancements for their current or any
lower tier. In addition, reaching a new tier gives the characters additional stat
increases defined for each tier. Each new tier gives the character +1 VL, +1 SL, +1
attribute point and +1 DP maximum. Tiers beyond tier 5 only give +1 VL and +1 SL.
Advancements
Advancements are additional upgrades gained through levels with each new level
allowing 2 advancements to be chosen from the current and all previous character
tiers. All tiers have at least these available advancements to choose from:
[x1] +1 ACC
[x1] +1 EVA
[x2] +2 VL
[x2] +2 SL
[x4] Learn new discipline ability
Other advancements are available in specific tiers only:
[x1] Unlock a new aspect slot - Tiers 1-5
[x1] Learn a new discipline - Tiers 1-4
[x1] Increase a conviction to rank 5 - Tier 4
[x1] Increase a skill to rank 5 - Tier 5
